analysis.one_liner: Limits health insurers' profits, caps drug copays, expands subsidies, and bans surprise emergency billing.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tighten rules on health insurance across the board. It would require insurers to spend at least 85 cents of every premium dollar on medical care, let regulators block premium increases deemed unreasonable, and cap prescription drug copays at $250 a month per person. It would expand ACA premium subsidies to higher incomes, ban surprise bills from out-of-network emergency rooms, and pull loosely regulated association and short-term plans under the same consumer protections as regular insurance. It never left the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own insurance, families caught paying full price for employer coverage for a spouse or child (the 'family glitch'), patients with high drug costs, and anyone hit with an out-of-network emergency room bill.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insurance buyers, patients with drug costs, ER patients

how_it_helps.text: Raises the medical loss ratio floor from 80% to 85%, so insurers must spend at least 85 cents of every premium dollar on actual medical care rather than overhead and profit.
Requires regulators to review premium increases and allows them to prohibit increases found unreasonable, and bars insurers from hiding rate-filing information behind trade secret claims.
Caps prescription drug cost-sharing at $250 per month per person and $500 per family, with the cap indexed to medical inflation after 2020.
Expands ACA premium tax credits to households above 400% of the poverty line and calculates the subsidy against a gold-level plan, while lowering required premium contributions on a sliding scale.
Fixes the 'family glitch' so that a family member who cannot get affordable employer coverage for themselves can qualify for exchange subsidies.
Makes primary care, specialist visits, mental health and substance-use outpatient care, generic drugs, and urgent care exempt from deductibles in standardized plans.
Bans out-of-network emergency providers from balance billing patients beyond normal in-network cost-sharing.
Requires plans to cover services from out-of-network providers at in-network cost-sharing when no in-network provider is reasonably available, and when a patient relied on a wrong provider directory.

Protects continuity of care when a plan drops a provider mid-treatment, prohibits mid-year removal of drugs from formularies or mid-year copay increases, and requires 30 days notice before a provider termination.

Treats association health plans sold to individuals as individual insurance and shuts down the Labor Department's proposed rule expanding association plans, and reclassifies short-term limited-duration plans so they fall under the same consumer protections as regular coverage.

Establishes federal network adequacy standards covering provider counts, travel distance, and appointment wait times, and requires Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed-care organizations to offer exchange plans in areas with fewer than three insurers.
Extends open enrollment periods to at least eight weeks, funds $480 million in enrollment marketing for 2019 with increases after, and requires nonprofit consumer groups to receive navigator grants.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, hospitals and physicians who currently bill patients for out-of-network emergency care, and taxpayers who would fund the expanded subsidies and enrollment programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, emergency-care providers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates open-ended federal money: 'such sums as may be necessary' for enhanced cost-sharing reductions plus $480 million for marketing in 2019 with guaranteed 4% annual increases, all without an offset, adding to federal deficits.

A stricter medical loss ratio and stronger rate review can squeeze insurer margins in markets with little competition, and insurers that exit a state can leave consumers with fewer plan choices rather than cheaper plans.
Basing subsidies on a gold plan and letting anyone above 400% of poverty claim a credit draws more federal spending toward middle- and upper-income households, raising the bill's total cost.

Forcing Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed-care organizations to offer exchange plans in low-competition areas is an unusual cross-program mandate that those insurers and their federal contracts did not previously carry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are the strongest part of the bill and address real, well-documented harms: surprise emergency bills, mid-year coverage losses, and junk short-term plans. The affordability provisions are generous but costly, relying on uncapped appropriations and richer subsidies that benefit higher-income households too. An honest supporter would concede the bill's price tag and its risk of pushing some insurers out of thin markets; an honest opponent would have to concede the balance-billing ban and continuity-of-care rules protect patients who get hit hardest today.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2019, with no hearing, markup, or vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Warren introduced the bill on March 21, 2018, with five Democratic cosponsors and one Independent, Senator Sanders.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action appears in the record: the Finance Committee held no hearing or markup on the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers keep the current 80% payout floor and their trade-secret protections on rate filings, and hospitals and emergency physicians keep the ability to balance-bill patients for out-of-network emergency care. Consumers gained nothing because none of the protections took effect.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Democrats plus Senator Sanders, who caucuses with Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee took no action, but no one ever cast a vote against the bill on the merits.

industries.note: The bill raises the medical loss ratio floor to 85%, gives regulators power to block premium increases and opens rate filings to public disclosure, imposes network adequacy and drug cost-sharing caps, and pulls association and short-term plans under full regulation. Insurers' profits and pricing freedom under the status quo are exactly what the bill's protections would take from them.

The bill bans balance billing for out-of-network emergency services, requiring providers to accept in-network-equivalent payment instead of charging the patient the difference. It also forces coverage of out-of-network care at in-network rates in cases of directory errors and continuity-of-care.

industries.industry: Association health plan and short-term plan marketers
industries.note: The bill treats association plans sold to individuals as individual insurance and nullifies the Labor Department's proposed rule expanding association plans, while reclassifying short-term plans so they cannot escape ACA consumer protections. These channels exist largely to sell cheaper coverage with fewer protections.
